rv.q: As far as voyages into the unknown go, “A Fine Madness” is a worthy vessel.
New realizations about Thomas Jefferson and history will inevitably be heightened or reflected upon after seeing this provocative and sometimes polemical play.
In one breathtaking tableau, Parks distills the central contradiction of both the play and the nation itself.
The myriad contradictions and hypocrisies of life at Monticello are written on the wall in Round House's incisively funny production directed by Timothy Douglas.
"Sally & Tom,” a play about America’s conflicted past and present, is perfect for 2026, showing how history can sometimes repeat itself in new and provocative ways.
Again and again, Douglas and his cast beguile us with a stirring scene from 1790. Monticello, only to deflate the effect by snapping us back to the mundane present.
But in creating a self-conscious show, Parks loses the psychological terror that defines her strongest works.

cn.t: Parks' metatheatrical examination of Jefferson and Hemings earns praise for its perceptive, layered exploration of American myth and moral paradoxes, though critics remain somewhat divided on its overall impact.
